parole.significato: produces masculine nouns from feminines, usually signifying a male animal
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *īˀnas, from Proto-Indo-European *-iHnos. Compare the suffixes Old Prussian -ins and Proto-Slavic *-ьnъ in the words awins (“ram”) and *ovьnъ (“ram”) respectively.

parole.significato: Added to nouns or verbs to derive adjectives with the meaning 'typical of' or 'characterized by' the original noun: lik…
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *-kas, from Proto-Indo-European *-kos. Cognate with Latvian -īgs.

parole.significato: forms diminutives, usually from masculine nouns.
parole.testo: Palatalised variant of -ùkas, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *-ukas, from Proto-Indo-European *-kos; compare Latvian -uks, Proto-Slavic *-ъkъ. Compare Proto-Germanic *-ukaz > English -ock (hillock, bullock).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *-mō, *-men-; compare Latvian -mens, Old Prussian -men, Proto-Slavic *-mę. From Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥, *-men-, a neuter nominalising suffix. Cognates include Latin -men, Ancient Greek -μᾰ (-mă), Old Armenian -ումն (-umn).

parole.significato: Used to form genitive singulars of masculine a-stem nouns.
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *-ā; compare Latvian -a, Proto-Slavic *-a (“id”). From the Proto-Indo-European thematic masculine ablative ending *-ōd, with regular Balto-Slavic loss of final d. Compare Sanskrit -आत् (-āt), Latin -ō and Ancient Greek ὄπ-ω (óp-ō, “whence”). parole.significato: Used to form accusative plurals of masculine a- and u-stem nouns.
parole.testo: From an older *-uos (compare the pronominal ending -uosius). From Proto-Balto-Slavic *-ons; compare Latvian -us, Old Prussian -ans, Proto-Slavic *-y. From Proto-Indo-European *-ons (“accusative plural ending”), also reflected in Ancient Greek -ους (-ous), Latin -ōs, Sanskrit -आन् (-ān) and Gothic -𐌰

parole.significato: forms nouns with the meaning "collection of" or "area abounding in" the original noun
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *-īˀnas, from Proto-Indo-European *-iHneh₂ and *-eyneh₂.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *abōˀ (“both”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰóh₁, possibly prefixed with *Ho. Cognate with Latvian abi, Old Prussian abbai and Proto-Slavic *oba, and less directly with Sanskrit उभ (ubhá), Gothic 𐌱𐌰𐌹 (bai), Latin ambo (“both”) and Ancient Greek ἄμφω (ámphō, “both, f

Inherited from Old Lithuanian akis, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ak- (compare Latvian acs, Old Prussian ackis (“eyes”) (nominative plural), Proto-Slavic *oko), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ-. Cognate to Latin oculus, English eye.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *ákmō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éḱmō (“stone, rock”) (with the supposedly regular depalatalization of */ḱ/). Cognates include Old Church Slavonic камꙑ (kamy), Latvian akmens, Persian آسمان (âsmân), Sanskrit अश्मन् (aśman), Ancient Greek ἄκμων (ákmōn), English hammer. Doubl
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *akstis (*aštis?), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ-. Cognate with Latvian aksts (“prickle, sharp point”), Proto-Slavic *ostь.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *eśetis (whence also Latvian ecêšas, Old Prussian aketes, Proto-Slavic *esetь (“grain rack”)), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂oḱetis, a variant of *h₂oḱ-et-eh₂ (“harrow”), itself perhaps a derivative of *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”). Direct cognates include Ancient Greek ὀξίνα f (oxína, “ox-

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *algā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂elgʷʰ-. Cognate with Latvian àlga (“salary”), Old Prussian ālgas (“salary”, Gsg.), Ancient Greek ἀλφή (alphḗ, “gain, profit”), Sanskrit अर्घ (arghá, “worth, value, price”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *alk, from Proto-Indo-European *Heh₃l-. Cognate with Latvian ȩ̀lkônis.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *alu, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂elut-. Cognate with Latvian alus (“beer”), Old Prussian alu (“beer”), and Proto-Slavic *ȍlъ (“beer”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *anas (“yon”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énos (“yonder, otherwise”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *ángis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éngʷʰis (“snake”). Cognate with Latvian ôdze, Old Prussian angis (“snake”), Russian уж (už, “grass snake”), Latin anguis (“snake, serpent, dragon”), Old Armenian աւձ (awj, “snake, serpent”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *anˀglís, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óngʷl̥ (“coal”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *ánˀkas, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ónkos.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *anź-(u)-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂emǵʰ-u-. Cognate with Polish wąski (“narrow”), Gothic 𐌰𐌲𐌲𐍅𐌿𐍃 (aggwus), Latin angustus and Sanskrit अंहु (áṃhu-).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *ánˀtis, i-stem variant of Proto-Indo-European *h₂énh₂ts (“duck, aquatic bird”). Cognate with Old Prussian antis, Proto-Slavic *ǫtь, English annet.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *ántaras, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énteros. Cognate with Latvian ùotrs (“second”), Old Prussian antars (“second, other”), Proto-Slavic *vъ(n)torъ, Proto-Germanic *anþeraz, Sanskrit अन्तर (ántara).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *or-ei/i-, from Proto-Indo-European *Hor-eye-ti, a causative formation from *h₁er- (“to separate”). Cognate with Latvian ā̀rdît (“to destroy, scatter”), Proto-Slavic *oriti (“to tempt”), Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hárdʰas (“division, half”).

parole.significato: ard plough (simple plough consisting of a spike dragged through the soil.)
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *árˀtlan; compare Latvian ar̂kls, Proto-Slavic *òrdlo. From Proto-Indo-European *h₂(e)rh₃-tlom (“plough”), from *h₂erh₃- (“to plough”). The word is equivalent to arti (“plough”) + -klas; see for more. Cognates include Old Armenian արաւր (arawr), Old Norse arðr, Ancient Greek

parole.significato: prefix indicating movement towards something (esp. speaker)
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *at- (“back, away, from”) (compare the preposition *at, *ati), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eti (“beyond, over”). Cognate with Latvian at- (“away, open”), Proto-Slavic *otъ (“from”), Sanskrit अति (ati, “beyond, over”), Latin et (“and”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *atlaikas, from Proto-Indo-European *leykʷ-. Cognate with Proto-Slavic *otъlěkъ.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *augtei, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewg- (“to increase”). Cognate with Latvian aûgt (“to grow”), Latin augeō, Proto-Germanic *aukaną.

parole.significato: bootleg (the part of a boot that is above the instep)
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *aul-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewl-. Cognate with Latvian aũls (“leg of a boot”), Old Prussian aulis (“shin”), Proto-Slavic *ulica, Ancient Greek αὐλός (aulós), Proto-Germanic *eulaz.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *aum-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew-m-, a derivation of *h₂ew- (“to see, perceive”). Cognate with Old Church Slavonic оумъ (umŭ, “mind”) and indirectly Ancient Greek αἰσθάνομαι (aisthánomai, “to perceive”), Sanskrit आविस् (āvís, “openly, manifestly, evidently”), Latin audiō
Inherited from Old Lithuanian ausi̇̀s, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *auš-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ows-. Cognate to Latvian auss, Old Prussian āusins (accusative plural), Proto-Slavic *ȗxo.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *oušt- (*aušt-?, ultimately from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *h₁óh₃s (“mouth”), see also Latin ōs. Cognate with Latvian aũšât (“to chatter, talk nonsense”), Proto-Slavic *ustiti.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *áutei, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ew- Cognate with Latvian àut (“to put on footwear”), Proto-Slavic *uti (“to put on”) (> *jьzuti, *obuti), Hittite [script needed] (unu-, “to adorn, decorate, lay (the table)”) Latin *uō (“to put on”) (> exuō, induō).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *auštrā́ˀ (“dawn, morning”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ews-ro-, from *h₂ews-. Cognate to Latvian àustra, aũstra (“dawn light”), Proto-Slavic *utro (“morning”), Proto-Germanic *Austrǭ (“Easter, springtime”), Latin aurora (“dawn”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *aulios (whence also Latvian aũlis (“beehive”)), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewlós, nominal form of *h₂ewlo- (“tube, hole, channel”). Cognate with Proto-Slavic *ulьjь (“beehive; opening”), Ancient Greek αὐλός (aulós, “tube, pipe”), Latin alvus (“belly, beehive”), etc.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *awinas, a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *h₃éwis. Cognate with Old Prussian awins, Latvian àuns, Proto-Slavic *ovьnъ. Equivalent to avi̇̀s (“sheep”) + -inas.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *áwis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ówis.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *auˀis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwh₂os (“grandfather”). Cognates include Old Prussian awis (“uncle”); Russian уй (uj), Serbo-Croatian ујак, ujak < Proto-Slavic *ujь (“maternal uncle”), etc. The suffix -ýnas is of unclear formation. It may be linked to the identical suffix
auti (“put on shoes”) + -ėti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *awtei, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ew- (“put on, wear”). Cognate with Latvian aut, Proto-Slavic *uti (cf. Old Church Slavonic обути (obuti)).

From Old Lithuanian eš, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ēˀźun, *eś; compare Latvian es, Old Prussian es/as, Sudovian es, Proto-Slavic *(j)azъ. From Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵ-, *h₁eǵHom (“I”). Compare Sanskrit अहम् (aham), Ancient Greek ἐγώ (egṓ), Old Armenian ես (es), Latin egō. The final *-ś in Baltic is

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *aś-aka-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”). Cognate with Latvian asaka (“fishbone”), Polish osoka (“water soldier”), Russian осо́ка (osóka, “sedge”), Belarusian асака́ (asaká, “id.”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic (compare Latvian asara), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éḱru, perhaps from a compound *dr̥ḱ-h₂eḱru- (literally “eye bitter”) (compare *dáḱru-). Cognate with Ancient Greek δάκρυ (dákru), Sanskrit अश्रु (aśru), English tear.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *aśís, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs-.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *áśmō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éḱmō. Compare akmuõ, Latvian akmens and Latvian asmens. Doublet of akmuo.
From Old Lithuanian *ãštras (“sharp”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *aśras, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱrós (“sharp”) (compare Serbo-Croatian oštar, Slovene oster).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *aśtṓ (compare Latvian astoņi), from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw. Cognate to Old Church Slavonic осмь (osmĭ), Sanskrit अष्ट (aṣṭa), Latin octō.

PIE word  *h₁éḱwos From Proto-Balto-Slavic *éśwāˀ, an ā-stem derivation of Proto-Indo-European *h₁éḱwos (“horse”). Cognate with Old Prussian aswinan (“mare's milk”), Sanskrit अश्व (áśva), Latin equus, Ancient Greek ἵππος (híppos).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *baigtei, probably from Proto-Indo-European *bʰ-né-g-ti ~ *bʰ-n̥-g-énti, the nasal-infixed present form of *bʰeg- (“to break”). However, the circumflex accent of the Lithuanian word is strange, as Winter's law predicts an acute accent.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *bolˀ-n-, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰolH-n-. Cognate with Proto-Slavic *bolna.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *bálˀtas (“faint, white”) (compare Latvian balts), which is generally derived from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“white”) and compared with Proto-Slavic *bòlto (“swamp; mud”); see there for more discussion on the root. Compare also Proto-Slavic *bělъ (“white”).
Cognate with Latvian banga (“wave; crowd; cloud”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *bangā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeg- (“to bend”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *bárˀnis, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH-.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *bárˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH-.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *bardā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰardʰeh₂.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *basás, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰosós. Cognate with Latvian bass, Russian босо́й (bosój), English bare.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *beź, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰe (instrumental particle) + *-ǵʰs (“out”). Cognate with Proto-Slavic *bez(ъ) (“without”); see there for more cognates.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *bebrus, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰébʰrus. Cognate with Latvian bȩbrs, English beaver.
Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *bértei (possibly *bérˀtei), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to carry”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *berźas, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerHǵós. Cognate with Proto-Slavic *berza, Latvian bȩ̃rzs, bẽrze, Old Prussian berse, English birch.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *bed-, *bod-, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰedʰh₂-, *bʰodʰh₂-. Cognate with Latvian best (“to dig, bury”), Old Prussian embaddusisi (“they stick”), Proto-Slavic *bosti (“to stab, sting”), and Latin fodio (“to dig”).

parole.significato: to fear; to be afraid of
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *bajā́ˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰoyh₂-eh₂-ti, from *bʰeyh₂-.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *bitīˀ (compare Latvian bite), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰey-, *bʰī-. Cognate to English bee.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *blaiˀd-(w)á-s, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰloyd-(w)ó-s. Cognate with Proto-Slavic *blědъ, Proto-Germanic *blaitaz.

parole.significato: cloudiness, obscuration of mind or eyesight, drowsiness
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *blandás, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlendʰ-. Cognate with Latvian blods, Proto-Slavic *blǫdъ (“delusion”), Icelandic blundr (“slumber”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *bljouʔ-, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlewH-. Cognate with Latvian bļaût, Proto-Slavic *bľьvati, Ancient Greek φλέω (phléō), Latin fluo.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *bliskas, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰliǵ-sko-. Equivalent to blizgė́ti (“to shine”) + -as. Cognate with Proto-Slavic *blěskъ, *blьskъ.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *blúšāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlúseh₂.
Fom Proto-Balto-Slavic *brauktei, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrewḱ- (“to poke, thrust, throw”). Cognate with Latvian bràukt.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *bréidis, from a Proto-Indo-European *bʰreydʰ- (“elk, deer”). Cognate with Latvian briêdis (“elk”), Old Prussian braydis (“elk”) (< *breidis); outside of Baltic, cognate with Sudovian brid (“deer”), Elfdalian brinde (“elk”), Swedish brinde (“elk”), Ancient Greek βρένδος (brén
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *brínktei, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrenk-. Cognate with Proto-Slavic *bręknǫti and Old Norse bringa (“chest”, noun).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *bred- or *bird-, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰredʰ- (“to wade”). Cognates include Latvian brist (“to wade”), Polish brnąć (“to wade”), Russian брести́ (brestí, “to stroll pensively”), and Albanian bredh (“to wander”).

Haplology of broterė́lis ‘little brother’, diminutive of *bróter- (in broterỹstė ‘brotherhood’, bróterautis ‘to fraternize, ally’), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *brā́ˀtē (compare Old Prussian brāti), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr. Another haplological form is dialectal brotis ‘brother’, but with pr
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *bruś/k-, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰruḱ-. Cognates include Bulgarian бръсна (brăsna, “to shave”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *burˀnāˀ, often thought to be from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH- (“to bore, pierce”), the “mouth” being perceived as a “hole, opening”. Cognate with Latvian pur̂ns (“snout”), Bulgarian бърна (bărna, “lip”); more distant cognates may include Armenian բերան (beran, “mouth”), Old

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *bḗˀgtei; cognate with Latvian bêgt, Proto-Slavic *běťi (“to flee, run”). From Proto-Indo-European *bʰégʷeti, from *bʰegʷ- (“run, flee”), with long vowel due to Winter's Law. Cognate with Ancient Greek φέβομαι (phébomai, “flee, take flight”). Possibly also Tocharian A pukäl,

Inherited from Old Lithuanian bū́ti, fromProto-Balto-Slavic *bū́ˀtei; present tense forms are from Proto-Indo-European *h₁es- (“to be”); suppletive stem forms derive from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to become”). Compare identical situation in Old Church Slavonic бꙑти (byti). Cognate to Latvian bût,

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *dabāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰabʰ-eh₂, from *dʰabʰ- (“to fashion, fit”); related to dabà (“nature, character”). Cognate with Polish doba (“twenty-four hours”), Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌳𐌰𐌱𐌰𐌽 (gadaban, “to happen; to be suitable”), Latin faber (“artisan”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *dainā (compare Latvian daĩn̨a), from *deî- (“to sing, dance”) (compare Latvian diêt), probably from Proto-Indo-European *deyh₁- (“move swiftly”) (compare Old Irish dían (“fast”), Ancient Greek δίω (díō, “to run away, flee”), Sanskrit दीयति (dīyati, “he soars”)). Also, compar
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *dáljāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *delh₁-. Cognate with Latvian daļa (“part; share”), Proto-Slavic *doľa (“share; fate”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *degtéi, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰégʷʰeti (“to burn”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *degut(j)as, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰ-.

parole.significato: cover (place or be over or upon)
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *deng-, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰengʰ-, *dʰn̥gʰ- (“to cover, conceal”). The original meaning of "dress, cover" is preferable to Mažiulis's suggestion of "bend" (cf. dangà (“arc”)), in view of Ukrainian одягти́ (odjahtý, “put on, wear”), Old High German tungen (“oppress, ma

From a previous undeclinable Eastern Baltic *dewin-, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *néwin, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥, *néwn̥ (“nine”). Probably from the same stem as *néwos- (“new”); apparently Proto-Indo-European had a base 4 numeric system, so that, after two 4's (= 8), 9 was the first (“new”) t

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *déśimt with a suffix -(t)i-s marking collective number (“group of ten”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥t (“ten”). Cognates include Latvian desmit and Latgalian desmit.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *dein- (oblique stem *din-); compare Latvian dìena, Old Prussian deinan (acc. sg.), Proto-Slavic *dьnь. The ablaut in Balto-Slavic suggests an original Proto-Indo-European n-stem *déy-n- (genitive *din-és (“day”)); compare Old Irish denus (“period of time”), Sanskrit मध्यन्दि

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *dírāˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *der- (“to split, flay”). Cognate with Latvian dīrāt (“to flay”), Polish drzeć (“to tear; to flay”), Russian драть (dratʹ, “to tear”), Gothic 𐌳𐌹𐍃𐍄𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌰𐌽 (distairan) and Ancient Greek δέρω (dérō). See also dirvà (“soil”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *dirˀwāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *dŕ̥Hweh₂. Cognate with Latvian dirva, Russian дере́вня (derévnja, “village”) and Sanskrit दूर्वा (dū́rvā-, “panic grass”). See also di̇̀rti (“to flay”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *draugás, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrewgʰ-.

Proto-Balto-Slavic *drugā́ˀtei, reflecting Proto-Indo-European *dʰrewg-/*dʰrewgʰ- (“to shake off, to drain”). Compare some Slavic languages (Polish drgać (“to tremble”), dreszcz (“shudder”), Russian дрожь (drožʹ, “shivering”)).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *dubus, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰéwbʰ-us, from the root *dʰewbʰ-. Compare Latvian dôbs.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *dúbna with a dissimilatory change from */bn/ to /ɡn/, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰubʰnós. Cognate with Old Prussian dubnas (“bottom”), Old Church Slavonic дъно (dŭno, “bottom”). Compare English deep.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *duktḗ (compare Old Prussian duckti, Proto-Slavic *dъťi, Finnish tytär), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰugh₂tḗr.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *dumˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰemH-. Cognate with Polish dąć (“to blow”) and Sanskrit धमति (dhámati, “to blow”). See also dùmplės (“bellows”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *dṓˀnāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰoHnéh₂.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *dṓˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *dédeh₃ti (“to give”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *durˀtei (whence also Latvian dur̃t (“to stab, prick”)), traditionally derived from an alternative zero-grade of Proto-Indo-European *der- (“to split, flay”) (whence di̇̀rti (“to flay, peel, flog”) and its ancestor, Proto-Balto-Slavic *dírāˀtei). From Proto-Balto-Slavic *dwírs, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwer-.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *dwideśimt (“twenty”), from Proto-Indo-European *dwi(h₁)dḱm̥ti (“twenty”). By surface analysis, dvi (“two”) + dešimt (“ten”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *dīkas, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰiHkos, according to Pokorny, from *deyh₁- (“to chase away, swing”). Cognate with Latvian dīks (“empty”), Proto-Slavic *dikъ (“wild”). Could be a borrowing from Slavic, but the difference in meaning is significant.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *dēˀd-, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁dʰos. Cognate with Latvian dȩ̀ds (“old man”), Proto-Slavic *dě̀dъ (“grandfather”), Ancient Greek τήθη (tḗthē, “grandmother”). Probably originally an onomatopoeia of babies' speech.

parole.significato: to place, to lay, to put
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *dḗˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *edlis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁edʰ-l (“spruce tree”), potentially of substrate origin. Cognate with Latvian egle (“spruce, fir”), Old Prussian addle (“spruce, fir”), Proto-Slavic *ȅdlь (“spruce”), Latin ebulum (“danewort”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *eitei, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁éyti.
Cognate with Proto-Slavic *oldi. From Proto-Balto-Slavic *aldjāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂oldʰeh₂; *h₂eldʰeh₂.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *elénjas, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁el- (“red deer, elk”). Cognate with Latvian al̂nis, Proto-Slavic *(j)elenь, Ancient Greek ἔλαφος (élaphos, “deer”), Old Armenian եղն (ełn, “hind”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *arélis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃érō. Common Balto-Slavic; compare Proto-Slavic *orьlъ. Compare to Latvian cognate ḕrglis.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *ašerā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱereh₂, from *h₂eḱ- (“sharp, pointed, angular; stone”).

Cognate with Latvian gals (“tip, end”), Old Prussian golis (“death”); from Proto-Balto-Slavic *galas, likely originally an o-grade action noun with meaning “demise” from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelH- (“to inflict, to project”), and related to root-verb gélti (“to hurt, to sting”). Related to galėti (“to be able”), Proto-Slavic *golěmъ (“powerful”), likely Proto-Celtic *galā (“ability”). From Proto-Balto-Slavic *galḗˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *gelH-.

parole.significato: to be able to; can, may
parole.testo: galia + -ėti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *galḗˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *gelH- (“able, powerful”), related to Proto-Slavic *golěmъ (“big”), as well as Proto-Celtic *galnati (“to be able”) (whence Welsh gallu (“to be able”)) and *galā (“ability”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *gánīˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰen-, *gʷʰon- (“to strike, to slay”); See also Latvian ganît (“to herd”), Proto-Slavic *gonìti (“to chase”), Russian гони́ть (gonítʹ, “to persecute”), Polish gonić (“to chase”); also Ancient Greek θείνω (theínō, “to kill”), Sanskrit हन्त

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; disputed; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: to get, to obtain, to gain
parole.testo: Of uncertain origin. Traditionally derived from Proto-Balto-Slavic *gáuˀtei, *gū́ˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷew(H)- (“to gain”). Cognate with Latvian gaut, gūt (“to catch, gain”), Old Prussian pogaūt (“to receive”), and (per Trubačev) Proto-Slavic *gyti, *guviti (“to acquire”). Outside of Balt
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *gedḗˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰedʰ-. Cognate with Proto-Slavic *žęděti.

parole.significato: to desire, to crave, to covet, to lust after
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *géistei, *gístei, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeidʰ-ie-, from *gʰeydʰ- (“to yearn for”). Cognate with Latvian gaidīt (“to wait”),Old Prussian gẽide (“id”), Proto-Slavic *žьdàti (“to wait, expect”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *gilˀtás, From Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃-.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *gerˀtlán, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerh₃-tló-m, from *gʷerh₃- (“to devour, swallow”). Cognate with Polish źródło (“source”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *gerˀtei (“devour, lap up”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerh₃- (“to devour”); compare Latvian dzer̂t (“drink”), Proto-Slavic *žèrti (“to devour, glut”) (Old Church Slavonic пожрѣти, пожьрѫ (požrěti, požĭrǫ, “swallow, devour”), Polish żreć (“eat greedily”), Russian demotic наж
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *gerˀ(ō)was, from Proto-Indo-European *gerh₂- (“to cry hoarsely; crane”). Cognate with Proto-Slavic *žeravь (“crane (bird)”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *gāˀi-, from Proto-Indo-European *g⁽ʷ⁾eH- (“to sing, cry”). Cognate with Latvian dziêdât (“to sing”), Proto-Slavic *gajati (“to caw, croak”), Sanskrit गायति (gāyati, “sing”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰen-. Cognate with Latvian dzīt, Old Prussian guntwei, Polish gnać (“to rush”), Ancient Greek θείνω (theínō, “to kill”) and Sanskrit हन्ति (hánti, “to slay”). See also ganýti (“to graze”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *garā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH-. Cognates include Sanskrit गिरि (girí-, “mountain, hill”), Bulgarian гора́ (gorá, “woods”) and Polish góra (“mountain”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *gírˀnūˀs, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷréh₂wō (“millstone”), a form of Proto-Indo-European *gʷréh₂us (“heavy”). Cognate with English quirn.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *gírˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH- (“to welcome, greet, praise”). Cognate with Latin grātus (“welcome”), Old Church Slavonic жрьти (žrĭti, “to sacrifice”), Old Prussian girtwei (“to praise”), Sanskrit गृणाति (gṛṇā́ti, “to praise”).
Cognate with Latvian grauds (“grain, corn”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic [Term?], from the Proto-Indo-European root *gʰrewd-, an extended form of *gʰrew-, itself from *gʰer- (“to grind”).
Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *gṓdas, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰedʰ- (“to gather”). Cognate with Latvian gùods.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *gúrˀtlan, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerh₃-; see gerklė (“throat”). Cognate with Polish gardło (“throat”)

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *gī́ˀšlāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰíH(s)leh₂-. Cognate with the second part of Old Prussian pette-gislo (“back vein”), Latvian dzīsla (“vein”), Proto-Slavic *žila (“vein, tendon”). Doublet of failas.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *gīˀw- (“to live”) (with semantic shift "to live" > "to recover and heal"), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷeih₃w- (“id”). Cognate with Latvian dzīvot, Proto-Slavic *živěti, *žiti, Sanskrit जीवति (jī́vati), Latin vīvō (“to live”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *gīˀwás (compare Latvian dzīvs), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós, cognate with Old Church Slavonic живъ (živŭ), Sanskrit जीव (jīva), Latin vīvus, Old English cwic.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *gīw-, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷeyh₃-. Cognate with Latvian dzīvot, Proto-Slavic *živěti, *žiti, Sanskrit जीवति (jī́vati), Latin vīvō (“to live”) (infinitive vīvere).

parole.significato: to search, look for (attempt to find that which is lost)
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *(a)iˀskāˀtei; compare Latvian iẽskât (“to search for lice”), Proto-Slavic *jьskàti (“to look for”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂i-sḱé-ti, the present of *h₂eys- (“to wish, desire”). Cognates include Proto-West Germanic *aiskōn (“to demand, question, claim”), Sansk
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *dílˀgas, from Proto-Indo-European *dl̥h₁gʰós.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *iˀst-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂id-st(h₂)-es-. Cognate with Latvian ikstis (“kidneys”), Old Prussian inxcze (“kidney”), Proto-Slavic *jьsto (“id”) (whence Old Church Slavonic исто (isto, “kidney; entrails”)), Proto-Germanic *aistô (“testicle”); see the Proto-Germanic for

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *ir (“and, also”), compare Latvian ir, Old Prussian ir (“and, even”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂r̥- (“thus, so”); compare Ancient Greek ἄρα (ára, “so, then, consequently”). From Proto-Balto-Slavic *jau, from Proto-Indo-European *ís and *Hyós (“that, who”). Cognate with Latvian jàu and Polish już; outside of Balto-Slavic, compare Gothic 𐌾𐌿 (ju, “already”), Latin iam (“id”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *jauˀnás, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yuh₁en-. Compare Latvian jaûns.
Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *jewas/*jawas, from Proto-Indo-European *yéwos. Akin to Proto-Slavic *jevinъ (“granary”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *jā́ˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *yeh₂-.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *jū́ˀga, from Proto-Indo-European *yugóm.

parole.significato: to get used to, to get accustomed
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *junk-, an infixed variation of *juk-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ewk-. Cognate with Latvian jûkt.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *yōˀs-, from Proto-Indo-European *yeh₃s- (“gird”) Cognates include Latvian josta (“belt”), Polish pas (“belt”) and Russian по́яс (pójas). Compare Ancient Greek ζωστήρ (zōstḗr).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *jūˀs, from Proto-Indo-European *yúHs (“you (pl.)”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *kai; compare Old Prussian kāi (“when”), Latvian kâ(i) (“when”), Old Church Slavonic цѣ (cě, “and also, besides”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷoy; compare Ancient Greek ποῖ (poî, “whereto”). From Proto-Balto-Slavic *káimas, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóymos (“village, home”), whence also Latvian ciems, Proto-Germanic *haimaz (“village”), Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌹𐌼𐍃 (haims, “village”), English home, ham (obsolete except in village names). Compare šeima, kiẽmas.

parole.significato: price (cost required to gain possession of something)
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *kainā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷoynéh₂.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *kākā, from Proto-Indo-European *kakka-.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *kaklas (compare Latvian kakls), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷékʷlos (“circle, wheel”). Doublet of ciklas.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *kalˀnas (compare Latvian kal̂ns, possibly Polish czółno (“dugout”) < *čьlno), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *kelH- (“lift; hill”), see Lithuanian kélti (“raise, lift”), ki̇̀lti (“rise, originate”), Polish czoło (“forehead, front”). Cognate with English hill <
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *kamanēˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *kemH-. Compare Latvian kamene and Latgalian kamane.

Per Derksen, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kamptas (whence also Proto-Slavic *kǫ̃tъ (“corner”)), from Proto-Indo-European *kamp- (“to bend, be crooked”). Cognate with Latin campus, Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌼𐍆𐍃 (hamfs). Also compare Proto-Celtic *kantos (“corner”), Ancient Greek καμψός (kampsós, “crooked, bent”). The sen

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *kam⁽ˀ⁾as, from Proto-Indo-European *kem- (“to press”), see also kamuoti (“to torture”), Proto-Germanic *hamjaną (“to hinder, obstruct”). Probably cognate with Latvian kamols and Russian ком (kom).

Inherited from Old Lithuanian kañklės. Further etymology is unclear, probably derived from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kankl- < *kantl-, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂n- (“to sing”), compare similar Proto-Celtic *kantlom, however, initial vowel doesn't match; because of that Smoczyński suggests non

parole.significato: a wart, verruca (on the skin, a plant, a toad, etc.)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Smoczyński suggests Proto-Balto-Slavic *skarpā- (from which also Proto-Slavic *xorpa), from zero-grade stem of Proto-Indo-European *skerp- (“to cut off, rip off”). Related to kir̃pti. Cognate with Latvian kãrpa.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *kárˀwāˀ (“cow”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱorh₂-weh₂, from *ḱerh₂- (“head, top; horn”), with an irregular depalatalization of the *ḱ. Cognate with Old Prussian curwis (“ox”), Proto-Slavic *korva (“cow”), English hart; see the Proto-Slavic for more on the phonetic developmen
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *kas, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷos.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *kāˀsā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *kes- (“to comb, scratch”). Cognate with Proto-Slavic *kosa (“hair”), Old Prussian kexti (“braided hair”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *káuˀlas, from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂ulós.
Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kā́ˀupas m, from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂wp-os, from *keh₂wp- (“heap, pile”). Cognate with Proto-Slavic *kùpъ (“heap, mound”), Proto-Germanic *haupaz (“heap”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *ker-, *kēr-, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷer-. Cognate with Proto-Slavic *čarъ (“magic, sorcery”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *ketū́res, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres.

parole.significato: to stuff, to cram, to fill
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *kimśtei (“to cram”), apparently from a Proto-Indo-European *k⁽ʷ⁾emḱ- (“to cram”), but without any known cognates outside of Balto-Slavic. Cognate with Proto-Slavic *čę̑stъ (“frequent, dense”) (whence Polish częsty (“id”)); the past passive participle form of this verb, kim̃š
PIE word  *kʷŕ̥mis From Proto-Balto-Slavic *kírmis, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷŕ̥mis. Cognate with Proto-Slavic *čьrvь, Latvian cirmenis.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *kiršnas, from Proto-Indo-European *kr̥snós (“black”). Cognate with Old Prussian kirsnan (“black”), Proto-Slavic *čьrnъ (“black”), Sanskrit कृष्ण (kṛṣṇá, “black”).
Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kirstei, derived from a t-extension of Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”).

Cognate with Latvian cìrvis, possibly dialectal Russian черв (červ, “sickle”), черва́к (červák, “saw”). Derksen reconstructs Proto-Balto-Slavic *kirw(i)os, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”), cf. ski̇̀rti, kir̃pti. Compare also Estonian kirves (“axe”).

Cognate with Proto-Slavic *klonъ (“fold, bend”). From Proto-Balto-Slavic *klánas, probably from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kel- (“to crook, to bend”). The original meaning was "a depression". klónis (“valley”) is from the same root.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *klā́ˀtei (“to lay, stack”), from Proto-Indo-European *kléh₂-ye-ti, the ye-present of *kleh₂- (“to put; to lay out”). Cognate with Latvian klāt (“to cover”), Proto-Slavic *klàsti (“to put, set down, stack”).

Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kaʔs(u)lio- (“cough”) (whence Latvian kãsulis, Russian ка́шель (kášelʹ), Polish kaszel), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂s- (whence also English whoost, Latgalian kōss, Sanskrit कासते (kā́sate)).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *kraujas, from Proto-Indo-European *krewh₂- (“blood of a wound”). Cognate with Old Prussian crauyo, Proto-Slavic *kry, Sanskrit क्रविस् (kravis), Greek κρέας (kréas).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *krauˀ-, from Proto-Indo-European *krewH- (“to pile, cover”). Cognate with Latvian kŗaut (“to heap, pile”), Proto-Slavic *krỳti (“to cover”); outside of Balto-Slavic, compare also Proto-Germanic *hreudaną (“to cover”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *kriā́u- + *-tlo-, from Proto-Indo-European *krewh₂- (“blood > hardened scab”). Cognates include Latin crusta, English crust, Irish crua (“hardened, tough”), Proto-Slavic *kruxъ (“fragile”). Compare kraũjas, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kráuja.
From kráuti, kráuna, króvė (“to heap, pile, load”) + -inỹs, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *krū́ˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *krewH-, *(s)krewH-.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *krušā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *krows-. Balto-Slavic cognates include Latvian krusa (“hail”), Proto-Slavic *krъxà (“lump”). Indo-European cognates include Ancient Greek κρούω (kroúō, “to beat”).

Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kulˀk-. Per Derksen, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷelh₁- (“to turn”). Cognates include Bulgarian кълка (kălka), Macedonian колк (kolk) and Serbo-Croatian кук.
Probably from earlier *kumpstis, metathesis from Proto-Balto-Slavic *punkstis, from Proto-Indo-European *pn̥kʷ-sti-s and therefore related to Proto-Slavic *pęstь and Proto-West Germanic *fūsti.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *kēr-, *ker-, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷr̥- (“to do, make, build”), probably via an extension *kʷr̥H- in order to account for the acute tone in the Baltic forms. Cognates include Latvian kur̃t (“to light, kindle”) and Sanskrit कृणोति (kṛṇóti, “to injure, do, make”). The app
Derived from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kū́ˀjas, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kewh₂- (“to strike”). Cognate with Old Prussian cugis and Proto-Slavic *kyjь (“stick”). See also káuti (“to slay”).

From an unattested *lagamas (“laid, placed”) + -inas (“nominal suffix”), the former component the present passive participle of an unattested *lagoti (“to lie down”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *lágīˀtei (“to lay (something)”), from Proto-Indo-European *logʰ-éye-ti, causative of *legʰ- (“to lie”). From Proto-Balto-Slavic *láiźīˀtei, causative/iterative of *léiźtei, from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵʰ-.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *lankás (“bow”), from Proto-Indo-European *lenk- (“to bend”), compare Latvian lanka (“lowland”), Old Prussian lunkis (“angle”). Cognates include Old Church Slavonic лѫкъ (lǫkŭ, “bow”), Belarusian and Russian лук (luk, “bow”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *lapijāˀ (compare Old Prussian lape, Latvian lapsa), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂(w)lṓp- ~ *h₂wl̥p- (“(red) fox”); compare Welsh llywarn (“fox”), Breton louarn, Ancient Greek ἀλώπηξ (alṓpēx), Armenian աղվես (aġves), Albanian dhelpër. From Proto-Balto-Slavic *laśas, from Proto-Indo-European *loḱs-os- (“salmon, trout”) or *laḱs-, cognate with Russian лосо́сь (losósʹ).

Related to Latvian lenta (“board, plank”), Proto-Slavic *lǫtъ (“linden bast”) (whence Russian лут (lut, “bast, bark of a linden”), also diminutive *lǫtъka), from Proto-Balto-Slavic [Term?], ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lenteh₂; compare Albanian lëndë (“timber; matter”), Proto-Germanic *lindō

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *ljáudis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁léwdʰis. More at English lede. The transitive pairing with lyti (“to rain”). Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *leˀitei, from Proto-Indo-European *leh₁i-. Cognates include Latvian liet, Old Prussian pralieton, Proto-Slavic *liti, and Ancient Greek λείβω (leíbō).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *leitus, from Proto-Indo-European *ley-, *lī- (“to pour, to flow, to drip”); see Latvian liêtus for cognates.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *lip-, from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to stick”). Cognate with Latvian lipt (“to stick”), Proto-Slavic *lьnǫti (“to stick”).

Derived from Proto-Balto-Slavic *laub-a-(s), from Proto-Indo-European *lowbʰ-ó-s, o-grade stem of *lewbʰ- (“to cut, peel”). Cognates include Latvian lobs (“bast, rind”), Latin liber (“bark of a tree”), English leaf, Proto-Slavic *lubъ (“bast”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *lekt-, from Proto-Indo-European *lek- (“to jump, scuttle”). Cognate with Proto-Slavic *letě̀ti (“to fly”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *leʔnas, *lēnas, from Proto-Indo-European *leh₁- (“soft, slow”). Balto-Slavic cognates include Latvian lȩ̃ns (“lazy”), lȩ̄̀ns (“lazy”), lȩ̂ns (“soft, mild”), Proto-Slavic *lěnъ (“lazy, slow”).

Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *lēˀtas, from Proto-Indo-European *leh₁-tos, from the root Proto-Indo-European *leh₁- (“slow”). Cognate with Latvian lēts (“inexpensive; (archaic) light, easy”) and probably Proto-Slavic *lěto (“summer”) (presumably, originally “mild, calm weather”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *lū́ˀśis, from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“shining, bright”). Cognate with Latvian lũsis, lũsa, lũse, Old Prussian luysis, and more distantly, Latin lynx and Ancient Greek λύγξ (lúnx)
Cognate with Latvian màiss (“bag”), Old Prussian moasis (“bellows”), Proto-Slavic *mě̑xъ (“leather bag”). From Proto-Balto-Slavic *maišás, from Proto-Indo-European *moysós (“fleece, skin”)
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *máiśīˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *meyḱ-. Cognate with Latin misceō, Sanskrit मिश्रयति (miśráyati), Old Church Slavonic мѣсити (měsiti).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *mélˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂-. Cognate with Latvian malt, Polish mleć, Old Armenian մալեմ (malem, “to crush”), Old High German malan (→ German mahlen), Hittite [script needed] (malla-), Old Irish meilid, Latin molere and Sanskrit मृणाति (mr̥ṇā́ti). See also smė̃l

A nursery word. From Proto-Balto-Slavic *mā́ˀmāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂-méh₂, a reduplication of *méh₂- - the root of *méh₂tēr (“mother”). Cognate with Proto-Slavic *mama, German Muhme (“aunt”), Latin mamma (“mother, nurse”), Irish mam (“mother”) among others.

parole.significato: to deem (to evaluate according to one's beliefs)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *mánīˀtei, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to think”).
* From Proto-Balto-Slavic *marjāˀs, from Proto-Indo-European *mor-i-. Cognate with Russian мо́ре (móre), Gothic 𐌼𐌰𐍂𐌴𐌹 (marei), Old Irish muir and Latin mare.

Related to mastýti and métyti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *met- (“to throw”). Pokorny proposed Proto-Indo-European *meh₁- (“to measure”) as further etymology. Cognate with Latvian masts (“casting of a net”).

Probably from Proto-Balto-Slavic *mat(r)ītei, from Proto-Indo-European *met- (“to cut, measure”), with semantic shift "to measure" > "to notice" > "to watch". Cognate with Proto-Slavic *motrìti (“to look at, watch”), *mětiti (“to mark, notice”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *m(a)ūˀ- (“to wash, submerge”), and cognate with Proto-Slavic *mỳti (“to wash”). Further origin outside of Balto-Slavic is uncertain; the root is generally reconstructed as Proto-Indo-European *mewH-, which Derksen and Fraenkel take to be the same as *m(y)ewh₁- (“to move”), w
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *maud- (“to think”), from Proto-Indo-European *mewHdʰ-. Cognate with Proto-Slavic *myslь (“thought”), Ancient Greek μῦθος (mûthos, “fact, purpose”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *maźas, from Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂s (“big, great”), with an inverted semantic shift from "big" > "small". Cognates include Latvian mazs.

Related to dialectal mēdžias (“forest, woods”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *medjas (genitive *meža, also yielding *meža-s by analogy), from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“middle; in-between”). For a parallel semantic connection between "trees" and "interiors", compare the relation between Old Norse við
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *medu, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰu. The noun was changed to a masculine noun; a more logical descendant would be neuter *medu.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *met-; according to Pokorny, from Proto-Indo-European *meh₁- (“to measure”). Cognate with Latvian mest (“to throw”), Proto-Slavic *mesti (“to throw; to sweep”) (whence Polish mieść (“to throw; sweep”)), and see the Proto-Slavic for more.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *meilas (compare Latvian mīls (“nice, sweet, dear, cherished, beloved”), Old Prussian mijls (“sweet, dear”), and Proto-Slavic *mìlъ (“soft, mild, gentle, agreeable, pleasant, sweet, dear”)), from Proto-Indo-European *meyh₁- (“soft, tender”). Cognate with Latin mītis (“weak, t
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *meiˀrás, from Proto-Indo-European *meyH-ró-s.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *míglāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃mígʰleh₂ (“mist, cloud”). Cognates include Latvian migla (“fog”), Polish mgła, Russian мгла (mgla), Albanian mjegull, Ancient Greek ὀμίχλη (omíkhlē).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *mílˀtas, from Proto-Indo-European *mlH-tó-s, from the zero-grade of *melh₂- (“to crush, grind”). Cognate with Latvian milti (“flour”), Old Prussian meltan (“id”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *mintís, from Proto-Indo-European *méntis (“thought”). Cognates include Old Church Slavonic памѧть (pamętĭ), Sanskrit मति (matí), Latin mēns and Old English ġemynd.

parole.significato: to die (used only for humans and bees)
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *mer-, *mir-. Compare Latvian mirt (“die”), Old Church Slavonic мрѣти, мьрѫ (mrěti, mĭrǫ, “die”), Russian умереть, умру (umeretʹ, umru, “die”). The Baltic forms are from the zero-grade of Proto-Indo-European *mer-, *mr̥- (“to die”). The -sta present was introduced at the Balt
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *mirtís, from Proto-Indo-European *mértis, from *mer- (“to die”). Cognate to Latin mors, mortis, Sanskrit मृत्यु (mṛtyú).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic [Term?] (whence also Latvian mirst, aizmirst, piemirst), from Proto-Indo-European *mer-s- (“to forget, neglect; to confuse, trouble”). Cognate with Sanskrit मृष् (mṛṣ, “to forget, neglect; to disregard”); see there for more cognates.

Back-formation from móterį (accusative singular of athematic fifth-declension mótė f (“wife; mother”)) reanalysed as third-declension and retaining genitive singular móters via suppletion, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *mā́ˀtē, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *mā́ˀtē, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr; cognate with Latvian mãte, Old Prussian mūti, Proto-Slavic *mati.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *mušjā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *mús-ih₂ ~ *mus-yéh₂-s, from *mus- (“a fly”). Cognate with Latvian muša, Old Church Slavonic моуха (muxa), Ancient Greek μυῖα (muîa), Latin musca, Old Armenian մուն (mun).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *nágas, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nṓgʰs (“nail”). Cognate with Latvian nags (“nail, claw”); see also nagà (“hoof”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *náktis, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *damús (“house”), from Proto-Indo-European *domos, from *dṓm. Cognate with Latvian nams, Proto-Slavic *dȍmъ, Latin domus, Ancient Greek δόμος (dómos), Sanskrit दम (dáma). The etymology seems rather secure despite the irregular sound change from *d- to *n-. The original d may
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *náujas, from Proto-Indo-European *néwyos.

parole.significato: no (used to show disagreement or negation)
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *ne, from Proto-Indo-European *né.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *neśtei (“carry, bring”); compare Latvian nest, Proto-Slavic *nestì. From Proto-Indo-European *h₁neḱ- (“carry, bring”); compare Tocharian B eṅk- (“take”) < *h₁n̥ḱ-, Ancient Greek ἐνεγκεῖν (enenkeîn, “bring”) < reduplicated present *h₁ne-h₁n̥ḱ-. This root seems to have frequen

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *neikas, equivalent to nie- + kas; compare Proto-Slavic *nikъto (“nobody”), *ničь, *ničьto (“nothing”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *né (“no”) + *kʷos (“what”) with an additional element, perhaps *éy (“he, the”); see jis (“he”). Cognate with Avestan 𐬥𐬀𐬈𐬗𐬌𐬱 (naeciš), O
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *nasús, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s-. Cognate with Latvian nāss, Proto-Slavic *nosъ, Sanskrit नासा (nā́sā), Latin nāris, nāsus, English nose.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *nōˀgás, from Proto-Indo-European *nogʷós.

Ultimately from Proto-Balto-Slavic *nṓmāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *nṓm-eh₂, from *nem- (“to give, to take”). Cognate with Latvian nuõma (“tax, quitrent”). Baltic borrowings are also Old Novgorodian наме (name), Livonian núom, Estonian nuum (“rent, lease”). Compare related Lithuanian núomoti, Latvi

parole.significato: and, but (used to express binary contrasts)
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *ō. Cognate with Latgalian a and Proto-Slavic *a (“and, but”). From Proto-Indo-European *h₁od; compare Sanskrit आत् (āt, “afterwards, then, so”), Avestan 𐬁𐬀𐬝 (āat̰, “afterward, then”), perhaps the ablative singular of *h₁e- (“demonstrative pronoun”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *ā́ˀbōl, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ébōl. Compare Proto-Germanic *aplaz (whence English apple), Russian я́блоко (jábloko), Bulgarian я́бълка (jábălka), Irish úll.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *āˀźina, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eǵ-í-no-s (“goatskin”). Compare Proto-Slavic *azьno, Sanskrit अजिन (ajina).

parole.significato: Comes along with po 'after', e.g. Grybšt pa-grybšt - grybšnis po grybšnio, bearing meanings 'after', 'definite', 'sligh…
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *pa, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂pó (“off, away”). Cognate with Proto-Slavic *po (“after, by”); see there for more.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *pos, from Proto-Indo-European *pós (“afterwards, post-”). Cognate with Proto-Slavic *pozdь́nъ (“late”), Latin post (“behind, after”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *patī, from Proto-Indo-European *pótnih₂. Cognate with Sanskrit पत्नी॑ (pátnī, “mistress, wife”), Ancient Greek πότνια (pótnia, “lady, mistress”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *patis, from Proto-Indo-European *pótis (“master, ruler; husband”). It is thought that the "lord" meaning is a derivative of an even older "self" meaning.
Derived from Proto-Balto-Slavic *w(e)iˀdēˀtei (lengthened zero-grade stem), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to see”). Cognate with Latvian pavīdet.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *peliā (compare Latvian pele (“mouse”), Old Prussian pele (“harrier”)), from Proto-Indo-European *pelH- (“gray”) (compare Lithuanian pálšas (“ashy gray”), pi̇̀lkas (“gray”)). The computing sense is a semantic loan from English mouse.
Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *pénki, from Proto-Indo-European *pénkʷe.

Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *per, inherited from Proto-Indo-European *per-. Cognates include Proto-Slavic *per-, Ancient Greek περί (perí, “around, about”, preposition), Sanskrit परि (pári, “around, about”, adverb), Latin per, English for.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *perkūnas, from Proto-Indo-European *perkʷunos, from *pérkʷus (“oak”). Compare Latvian pērkuons, Old Prussian Perkuns.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *perˀstei / *pirˀstei, from Proto-Indo-European *pérdetor. Cognate with Latvian pir̂st, Albanian pjerdh, English fart.
Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *p(e)iś-, from Proto-Indo-European *peyḱ- (“to paint, to mark, to color”). Compare Proto-Slavic *pьsàti.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *pilis, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁-í-s, from *tpelH- (“stronghold”). Cognate with Latvian pìls, Ancient Greek πόλις (pólis), Sanskrit पुर (pura).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *pílˀnas, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *pilˀtei, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁- (“to fill”). Cognate with Latvian pilt (“to drip, flow”) pilēt (“to drop, drip”), pildīt (“to fill”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *pínˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)penh₁-. Cognate with Latvian pīt, Polish piąć się (“to climb”) and Ancient Greek πένομαι (pénomai, “to toil”) (which apparently got generalized from some domestic work; compare Ancient Greek πήνη (pḗnē, “thread on the bobbin”) > Latin pā

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *pírˀmas, from Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- (“before, in front”), ultimately from *per- (“before”). Cognate with Old English fyrest (English first); Latin primus, Ancient Greek πρῶτος (prôtos) (Modern Greek πρώτος (prótos)).

Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *pištei, from Proto-Indo-European *pis-é-ti, from *peys- (“to crush”). Root cognate with Russian перепихну́ться (perepixnútʹsja), перепи́х (perepíx), перепихо́н (perepixón) (< пиха́ть (pixátʹ)).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *platús, from Proto-Indo-European *pléth₂us, from the root *pleth₂-. Cognates include Latvian plats, Old Prussian plat- (from a placename, Platmedyen, where median = “forest”), Sanskrit पृथु (pṛthu, “broad, wide, great, powerful”), Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “broad, wide,

parole.significato: to wash, to rinse; to bathe; to scrub
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *plauˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₃(w)-. Cognates include Ancient Greek πλέω (pléō, “to float”) and English flow.

Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *pláutja, from Proto-Indo-European *plew- (“to flow, float”); lungs were perhaps viewed as "floating objects" in an anatomical context. Cognate with Latvian plàušas, Proto-Slavic *plūťè (“lung”), Ancient Greek πλεύμων (pleúmōn, “lung; jellyfish”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *plúnksnāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *plúnksneh₂. Cognate with Latin plūma (“feather”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *pa (“after, by”) (compare Latvian pa, pa-, Old Prussian po (“after, by, under”), Proto-Slavic *po (“after, by, at”)), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂pó, *h₂epó (“away, from”). Other cognates include Mycenaean Greek 𐀀𐀢 (a-pu, “from”), Sanskrit अप (ápa, “away, off”), Old Persian

parole.significato: to wash (esp. one's face), to bathe
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *prus-sk-, from Proto-Indo-European *prews-. Cognates include Sanskrit प्रुष्णोति (pruṣṇoti, “to sprinkle”), Czech prskat (“to splutter, sizzle”) and Serbo-Croatian prskati (“to splash”).
Related to Lithuanian prie (“near”), Latvian priekša (“front”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *prei, from Proto-Indo-European *per-.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *put- (“small/young animal, bird”), cognate with Latvian putns (see there for more) and Old East Slavic пътица (pŭtica), Old Church Slavonic пътица (pŭtica) (< Proto-Slavic *pъtìca). Further potentially related to Sanskrit पोत (pota, “the young of an animal”) via Proto-Indo-E

parole.significato: cunt, pussy (the female genitalia, especially external genitalia)
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *pīˀsdāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *písdeh₂. Cognate to Latvian pīzda (“cunt”), Old Prussian peisda (“ass”), Proto-Slavic *pīzdà (“vagina”), Albanian pidh (“vagina; cunt”), Persian پیزی (pīzī, “ass, anus”).
Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *pūteiti, from Proto-Indo-European *púH-e-ti, from *puH- (“to decay, rot”). Cognate with Latvian pũt (“to rot”).
Adjectival derivation in -ùs, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *rámbas, from Proto-Indo-European *remb-. Cognate with Latvian robs, Proto-Slavic *rǫbъ.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *rad-; compare Latvian rast. Can be connected with Proto-Slavic *rodìti (“give birth”); compare the reflexive, rastis (“appear, arise”). Related to rasmė (“yield, harvest”). From Proto-Balto-Slavic *raudas, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rowdʰ-ós, from *h₁rewdʰ-. Cognates include Latvian ruds, Proto-Slavic *rudъ and English red.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *raudas, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rowdʰ-ós, from *h₁rewdʰ-. Cognates include Latvian ruds, Proto-Slavic *rudъ and English red. See also raũdas (“reddish-brown”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic [Term?], from Proto-Indo-European *HrewdH-. Cognate with Latvian raudāt, Russian рыда́ть (rydátʹ), Old English rēotan (“to weep; to complain”) and Sanskrit रोदिति (roditi, “to weep”).

parole.significato: to grub, to pull out (roots, stumps etc.)
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *ruʔ-, from Proto-Indo-European *(H)rewH-. Cognate with Latvian raût, Polish rwać (“to tear (flowers etc.)”) and ryć (“to burrow”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *rā́ˀdīˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂roh₁dʰéyeti, from *h₂reh₁-dʰh₁- (“to think, arrange”). Cognate with Latvian rãdît (“show, indicate”), possibly Old Church Slavonic радити (raditi, “take care of”). Compare Old Irish rádaid (“talk”), Gothic 𐍂𐍉𐌳𐌾𐌰𐌽 (rōdjan, “speak”), Ice
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *rāpā́ˀ, *rēpā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)rāp-éh₂, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)rā́ps, *(s)rḗps.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *rudas, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ- (“red”). Compare Latvian ruds.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *rīˀtás, likely continuing Proto-Indo-European *h₃riH- (“flowth, raise”) + *-tós. From the same root, but via different extensions, descend Proto-Slavic *rěka (“river”), Latin rīvus (“river”), Proto-Germanic *rīsaną (“to rise”). The meaning probably went from “to flow, to pas

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *salˀdus, from Proto-Indo-European *sh₂el-d-u-s, an extended form of *sh₂el-, *seh₂l- (“salt”); the *-d- may have been added by analogy with the *-d- in Proto-Indo-European *sweh₂d- (“sweet”). Compare the related verb sálti (“sweeten”), as well as Latvian salds, Proto-Slavic
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *swápnas, from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos. Compare Latin somnus, Sanskrit स्वप्न (svapna).

parole.significato: reflexive possessive pronoun; belonging to the subject of the sentence (regardless of gender or number)
parole.testo: From the root sav- (cf. savęs), related to Latvian savs, Old Prussian swais, Proto-Slavic *svojь. From Proto-Balto-Slavic *swaias, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swé. For the specific construction, see màno.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *sēˀg-, from Proto-Indo-European *se(n)g-. Cognate with Slovene sẹ́či (“to reach for”), Sanskrit सजति (sájati, “to cling to”) and Latin noun seges (“cornfield”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *sektei, from Proto-Indo-European *sékʷetor (“to be following”). Cognate with Latvian sekt (“to follow, succeed, thrive”).

Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *se(n)ktei (“to subside, dry out”), from Proto-Indo-European *snékti, from the root *sek- (“to dry out”). Cognate with Proto-Slavic *sęknǫti (“to dry out”); see there for more cognates.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *senas, from Proto-Indo-European *sénos (“old”). Compare Latvian sȩns.

Neologism from septyni̇̀ (“seven”), as an analogy to devyni̇̀ (“nine”) : deviñtas (“ninth”). Displaced Old Lithuanian sẽkmas, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *septmas, from Proto-Indo-European *septmós, compare Proto-Slavic *sedmъ.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *septín, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥. Cognate with Latvian septiņi, Old Church Slavonic седмь (sedmĭ), Sanskrit सप्त (saptá), Latin septem, Ancient Greek ἑπτά (heptá).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *swésō (compare Old Prussian swestro, Proto-Slavic *sestra), from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *sjū́ˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *syewH-. Cognate with English sew, Latin suo, Russian шить (šitʹ).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *(s)keit-, *(s)kait-, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kʷoyt-, Proto-Indo-European *(s)kʷeyt- (“to notice”). Cognate with Latvian skaitīt, Russian читать (čitatʹ, “read”), Sanskrit चेतति (cétati, “to perceive, take notice of”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *skírˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut off”). Cognate with Latvian šķir̃t (“to separate, divide, sever”).

Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *skī́ˀstas, from Proto-Indo-European *skid- + *-tós. Cognate with Latvian šķîsts (“thin, pure”), Old Prussian skijstan (“pure”) (sg. acc.), Proto-Slavic *čistъ (“clean, pure”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *smákras, from Proto-Indo-European *smóḱros, thematicized from an original neuter noun *smóḱwr̥, as continued by Hittite 𒍝𒈠𒀭𒆳 (za-ma-an-kur /⁠tsmá(n)gur⁠/).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *smirˀdḗˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)merd-.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *snáigas, from Proto-Indo-European *snóygʷʰos. See also sniegas (“snow”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *snáigas, from Proto-Indo-European *snóygʷʰos. Compare Old Church Slavonic снѣгъ (sněgŭ).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *sōdī́ˀtei (“to set, plant”), from Proto-Indo-European *sodéyeti (“to set, cause to sit”). Cognate with Latvian sâdinât (“to plant”), Old Prussian saddinna (“sets”), Proto-Slavic *sadìti (“to plant”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *parnas (“wing”), from Proto-Indo-European *pornóm (“wing, feather”). Cognate with English fern, Albanian fier (“fern”), Avestan 𐬞𐬀𐬭𐬆𐬥𐬀 (par^əna, “feather”), Sanskrit पर्ण (parṇá, “feather”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *sráutas, from Proto-Indo-European *srówtos, from the root *srew-.
Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *stábas, from Proto-Indo-European *stebʰ- (“to stay still”).

parole.significato: to be able, make an effort
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *sténgtei, from Proto-Indo-European *stengʷ-ye-ti, from *stengʷ- (“to push, thrust”), whence Latin stinguō (“to put out”) and English stink.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *śírˀnāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥h₂-néh₂, from *ḱerh₂- (“head, top, horn”), with an extra -n (from which also German Horn, English horn, Latin cornū and also cervus (“deer”)). More recently, it has been suggested that stirna might come from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“r
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *stāgas, from Proto-Indo-European *stog-os (“roof, covering”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *stāˀras (“old”), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂-ro-. Cognate with Russian ста́рый (stáryj, “old”), Old Norse stórr (“big”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *stā́ˀtis, from Proto-Indo-European *stéh₂tis (“standing, position”). Cognate with English station.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *stāˀwēˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *stā- < *steh₂- (“to stand”). Cognates include Latvian stāvēt, Old Church Slavonic ставити (staviti, “to put, to place”), Russian ста́вить (stávitʹ), Ukrainian ста́вити (stávyty), Bulgarian ста́вя (stávja, “to get up; to become; to suit,
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *trasdás, from Proto-Indo-European *trósdos, see also Latvian strazds, Old Prussian tresde, Latin turdus, Old Irish truit.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *sewk- (“turn, spin”), according to Pokorny, from Proto-Indo-European *sewh₁- (“to set in motion”). Compare Latvian sukt, Proto-Slavic *sъkati (Russian скать (skatʹ, “twist, turn”), Czech skati), and see the Proto-Slavic for more. Also related are Latvian sàucêt, Proto-Slavic
Ultimately from Proto-Balto-Slavic *śwaitas, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱweyt-. In this case, most likely a Slavic borrowing, likely from Old East Slavic свѣтъ (světŭ). Compare Samogitian sviets.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *sēdḗˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *sed-. Cognate with English sit.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *sḗˀstei, from Proto-Indo-European *sed-.
Nominal derivative of sū́ras (“salty”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *sū́ˀras, from Proto-Indo-European *súHros. Cognate with Old Prussian suris, Russian сыр (syr).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *takas, from Proto-Indo-European *tekʷ-. Cognate with Polish tok (“process”) and Avestan 𐬙𐬀𐬐𐬀 (taka, “course”). See also tekė́ti.

Plural of obsolete táukas, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *touʔkós, from Proto-Indo-European *towHk-o-, likely from *tewk-. Cognate with Latvian tàuki and Old Prussian taukis; further to Russian тук (tuk, “fat”), English thigh, and Old Irish tón (“rear end, buttocks”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *taurás, from Proto-Indo-European *táwros.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *t(j)autāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *tewtéh₂.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *tektei, from Proto-Indo-European *tek- (“to take, receive”). Cognate with Latvian tikt (“to become, attain, arrive (at), reach”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *tek-, from Proto-Indo-European *tekʷ-. Cognates include Latvian tecēt, Serbo-Croatian тећи/teći (“to flow”), Sanskrit तक्ति (tákti, “to rush”) and Old Irish teichid (“to flee”).
Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *temtei, from Proto-Indo-European *temH-.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *tilˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tl̥H-ti, from *(s)telH- (“to be still”), related to Old Irish tuilid (“to sleep”), Proto-Slavic *toliti.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *tintlas, from Proto-Indo-European *téntlom, from *ten- (“to stretch”). Cognate with Latvian tìkls (“net”), Old Prussian sasintinklo (“hare net”), Proto-Slavic *teneto (“net, snare”), Sanskrit तन्त्र (tántra, “loom”).

parole.significato: to investigate, to explore, to research
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *térˀtei, *tírˀtei, probably from Proto-Indo-European *tr̥h₁yéti, a yé-present of Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- (“to thread, to rub”) (some dialects show sta-present as well). Akin to Proto-Slavic *terti (“to rub, to scrape”), *těrati (“to seek”), Latvian trĩt (“to sharpen”). C
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *taˀkos, from Proto-Indo-European *teh₂-kos (“such”). Cognate with Proto-Slavic *takъ (“such”).
Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *tretias, from Proto-Indo-European *tr̥tyós.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *tríjes, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *tuˀ (“you”), from Proto-Indo-European *tuH. The oblique stem tav- has been generalized from the Proto-Indo-European genitive *téwe. For a discussion of the case endings, see àš (“I”).

Cognate with Latvian žul̂ts, Proto-Slavic *zьlčь. From Proto-Balto-Slavic *źulˀ-, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃-. The Lithuanian form underwent metathesis under the influence of tul̃žti (“to become wet, swell, be angry”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *tuskjas, from Proto-Indo-European *tews-. Related to Latvian tukšs, Russian то́щий (tóščij), Polish czczy, Finnish tyhjä, English thost, Persian تهی, Avestan 𐬙𐬎𐬯𐬆𐬥 (tusən), Sanskrit तुच्छ्य (tucchya).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *twirˀ- from a zero-grade of Proto-Indo-European *twerH-. Cognate with Latvian tvirts and Polish twardy (“solid”). Derksen does not give a full PBS reconstruction for this term, only noting that "the Baltic and Slavic suffixes do not match." Other cognates within Lithuanian:
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *twōrˀ-, from Proto-Indo-European *twōrH-. Cognate with Polish twarz (“face”). See also tvérti (“to seize”) and tvi̇̀rtas (“firm”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *tū́ˀsantis, from Proto-Indo-European *tuHsont-, *tuHsenti-. Akin to Latvian tūkstotis, Russian ты́сяча (týsjača), Polish tysiąc, English thousand, German tausend, Gothic 𐌸𐌿𐍃𐌿𐌽𐌳𐌹 (þūsundi).

Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *úngnis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁n̥gʷnís. The expected reflex of Winter's Law would have been blocked by the cluster -nCn-, compare vanduõ (“water”). However, see Proto-Slavic *vygъňь (“forge, hearth”) < *ūˀgnis.

Cognate with Latvian usna (“thistle”) and probably with dialectal Proto-Slavic *ušь (“carduoid”) (whence Old East Slavic оушь (ušĭ)), for Proto-Balto-Slavic [Term?] (“thistle”). Further origin uncertain. Possibly derived from the oblique ablaut-grade of Proto-Indo-European *wósHr̥ ~ *usHén-, whence
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *wed-, from Proto-Indo-European *wedʰ-.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *wed-, from Proto-Indo-European *wedʰ-.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *waiˀníkas, from Proto-Indo-European *woyh₁níkos. Cognate to Polish wianek (“garland”) and wieniec (“wreath”). See also výti (“to wind”), výtulas and vytùvai (“device to wind a thread”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *walˀdā́ˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂welh₁dʰh₁-, from *h₂welh₁- (“to rule”), compare Latvian vàldît, Proto-Slavic *volděti, Proto-Germanic *waldaną.
Cognate to Samogitian valstībė, Latvian valsts (“country”), Proto-Slavic *volstь (“power, authority”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *walˀstís, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂welh₁- (“to rule”).

Cognate with Old Prussian wolti (“ear (of corn)”), Proto-Slavic *voltъ/*voltь (“panicle”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *wolˀtis, from Proto-Indo-European *wolHt-. Related to Proto-Celtic *woltos (“hair”).

parole.significato: water (the substance; the surface of a body of water)
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *wandō (genitive singular *undnes); compare Latvian ûdens, Old Prussian wundan, Proto-Slavic *vodà. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wódr̥. The nasal infix is paralleled in Latin unda (“wave”), presumably analogically brought into the nominative from the oblique stem (cf.
Inherited from Old Lithuanian vãpsas, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *wápsāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *wóbʰseh₂. Cognate with English wasp.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *warda-, from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰo- (“word”). Cognate with Latvian vārds, English word and Latin verbum.

parole.significato: gate (movable part of a fence; large door)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *wárta n or *wártas m, which Derksen ultimately derives from Proto-Indo-European *wert- (“to turn, rotate”). Compare Latvian vārti, Old Prussian warto, Proto-Slavic *vorta; see the Proto-Slavic term for more theories.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *was(e)r, from Proto-Indo-European *wósr̥.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *waśkas, from Proto-Indo-European *wokso-, *woḱskom (“wax”). Cognates include Old Church Slavonic воскъ (voskŭ), Latvian vasks and Old English wæx (English wax).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *wéiˀdas, from Proto-Indo-European *wéyd-o-s, a nominalization of *weydós (“seen”) from *weyd- (“to see”).

Per Smoczyński, syncoped form of vẽlinas (“devil; demon”), derived from vėlė̃ (“ghost”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *weliā, from Proto-Indo-European *welh₃- (“to strike; to hit”). Cognate to Latvian vel̃ns; see Latvian veļi for more.

parole.significato: to vomit (to regurgitate the contents of a stomach)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *wémˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *wémh₁ti.
Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *werźtéi (“to bind, to strangle”), from Proto-Indo-European *werǵʰ-. Cognate with Proto-Slavic *verzti, *vьrzàti (“to tie”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *westéi, from Proto-Indo-European *wedʰ-. Cognates include Polish wieść (“to lead”), Russian вести́ (vestí, “to lead”), Slovene vésti Old Irish feidid (“to go, bring”), and English wed. Compare Latvian vest.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *wétušas, from Proto-Indo-European *wet-.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *widús (probably originally meaning separated, rural) presumably from Proto-Indo-European *weydʰ- (“to divide, wooded”). Cognate with Latvian vidus, Old Prussian widus (“boot stitch”). Further akin to Proto-Germanic *widuz (“wood”), Proto-Celtic *widus (“tree”), possibly Bulg

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *aiˀnas, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos. Baltic cognates include Latvian viêns, Latgalian vīns, Old Prussian ains. Indo-European cognates include German eins, Latin ūnus, Russian оди́н (odín), Polish jeden. The initial v- is typical for East-Baltic cognates and plausibly c
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *wilkás, from Proto-Indo-European *wĺ̥kʷos.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *wilkī́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *wl̥kʷíh₂s. Cognate with Old Norse ylgr (“she-wolf”), Sanskrit वृकी (vṛkī, “she-wolf”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *wílˀnāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wĺ̥h₁neh₂.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *wilˀn-, from Proto-Indo-European *welH- (“to turn, coil”). Cognate with Latvian vil̂nis, Proto-Slavic *vьlnà, Sanskrit ऊर्मि (ūrmi, “wave”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *wirt-, from the zero-grade *wr̥t- of the same Proto-Indo-European root *wert- as versti, vartyti. Cognate with Latvian virst, Old Prussian wirst (“he becomes”), Proto-Slavic *vьrtě̀ti (“turn”) > Russian вертеть (vertetʹ, “turn”), Serbo-Croatian vŕtjeti (“turn”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *wirˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to burn”). Compare Latvian vir̂t (“to boil”), Proto-Slavic *vьrěti (“to boil”), Hittite [script needed] (urāni, “burns”). An older theory from Pokorny suggests derivation from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wer- (“water, rain, flow”); see th
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *wíršus, from Proto-Indo-European *wers-. Cognate with Old Church Slavonic врьхъ (vrĭxŭ).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *wirˀźja- (along with Latvian virsis, Proto-Slavic *vȇrsъ), which Smoczyński derives from Proto-Indo-European *werḱ-. Most linguists agree on a non-Indo-European origin and describe Ancient Greek ἐρείκη (ereíkē) and Proto-Celtic *wroikos (“heather”) as non-Balto-Slavic cognat

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *wēweris, from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“squirrel; marten”). Cognate with Latvian vãvere, Old Prussian weware, Samogitian vuoverie, Polish wiewiórka and Latin vīverra (“ferret”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *wī́ˀras, from Proto-Indo-European *wiHrós. Baltic cognates include Old Prussian wijrs, Latvian vīrs. Indo-European cognates include Sanskrit वीर (vīrá), Latin vir, Old Irish fer.

parole.significato: spirit of a dead human; ghost
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *weliā, from Proto-Indo-European *welh₃- (“death”). Compare Latvian veļi.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *wēˀtrāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂weh₁-. Cognate with Proto-Slavic *větrъ (Old Church Slavonic вѣтръ (větrŭ, “wind”)), Old Prussian wetro (“wind”), Latvian vētra (“storm”).
Inherited from Old Lithuanian zuikis, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *źṓjinkas, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰey-.

Cognate with Latvian osa, Old Prussian ansis (“hook, latch”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ans-, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *h₂emseh₂ (compare Latin ānsa (“handle”), Proto-Germanic *ansijō (“handle, loop”)). Similarity with Proto-Germanic *ansaz (“beam”) has been discussed in the literature, alth

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *ēˀstei, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁édti (“to eat”). Cognate with Latvian ēst, Proto-Slavic *ě̀sti (whence Bulgarian ям (jam), Old Church Slavonic ꙗсти (jasti), Russian е́сть (jéstʹ)), English eat, Latin edō, Sanskrit अत्ति (atti), German essen, Old Norse eta (whence Swedish

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *in; compare Old Prussian en (“in, into”), Proto-Slavic *vъ(n) (“in, into”) from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én, *h₁n̥; compare Ancient Greek ἐν (en), Latin in, Proto-Germanic *in. From Proto-Balto-Slavic *śokˀāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱokh₂- (“wooden branch”). Cognate with Latvian sakas (“horse's collar”) and Sanskrit शाखा (śā́khā, “branch”); see the latter for more.

parole.significato: magpie (one of several species in the family Corvidae, especially the Eurasian magpie, Pica pica)
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *śárˀkāˀ. When compared with Ancient Greek κόραξ (kórax, “raven”) a Proto-Indo-European form *ḱor-h₂k- can be reconstructed, however they may well be independent formations. In any case, both forms ultimately go back to Proto-Indo-European *ḱer- (“crow, raven”), whence also,

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *śeimā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *tḱey-meh₂ (“settlement, village; family”), from the root *tḱey- (“to lie down; to settle, inhabit”). Cognate to Russian семья (semʹja, “family”), English home. Compare kaimas.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *śer(s)nos, from a Proto-Indo-European *ḱer(s)-no- (“frozen water”). Cognate with Latvian sȩ̄rsna (“hoarfrost”), Proto-Slavic *sẽrnъ (“id”), Old Armenian սառն (saṙn, “ice”), Proto-Germanic *herzną (“frozen snow”). The adjectival sense is an extension of the "frozen crust" sen
From from earlier *seši, Proto-Balto-Slavic *šéš (or *seš, without assimilation to final -š), from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs.
Assimilated from Proto-Balto-Slavic *žežkas, from Proto-Indo-European *g(ʰ)egʰ- (“ferret”), see also Proto-Indo-Iranian *ǰáǰʰukas (“hedgehog, polecat”).
From earlier *seštas (by analogy with cardinal number 6, šeši < earlier *seši), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *seśtas, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sweḱstós (ordinal form of *swéḱs).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *śḗˀweras; Proto-Balto-Slavic *śjáuˀras, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱeh₁wer-o- Cognate with Russian се́вер (séver, “north”) and Latin caurus (“north-western wind”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *śimta-, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm. Compare Latvian simts, Sanskrit शत (śata).
Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *śḗr, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱḗr.
From earlier širšuo, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *śirˀšṓ, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂s-. Cognate with English hornet.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *śís, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱís, an alteration of *ḱe (“this”). Cognates include Latvian šis, Old Prussian schis, sis, Proto-Slavic *sь, Gothic 𐌷𐌹𐌼𐌼𐌰 (himma) (dative), Latin cis (“this side of”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *ślaunis, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlównis (“buttocks”). Cognate with Sanskrit श्रोणि (śróṇi), Avestan 𐬯𐬭𐬀𐬊𐬥𐬌 (sraoni), Latin clunis, Old Norse hlaun, Welsh clun.

Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ślṓuˀtei, further perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlewH- (“to cleanse”) (whence Latin cluō (“to cleanse”), Ancient Greek κλύζω (klúzō, “to wash”)). Possibly related to dialectal Proto-Slavic *slavina (“valve, tap”) (if not a Latin borrowing) and hydronyms *Sluja

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *kwṓ (“dog”); compare Latvian suns, Old Prussian sunis (“dog”), Proto-Slavic *sùka (“bitch”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwṓ (“dog”). Cognate to Armenian շուն (šun), Sanskrit श्वन् (śvā́), Latin canis, Proto-Germanic *hundaz.
Cognate with Latvian svèts (“holy”), Old Prussian swints (“holy”), Proto-Slavic *svętъ (“holy”). From Proto-Balto-Slavic *śwentas (“holy”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwen- (“holy”).
From *ḱweyt- (“to shine”), possibly via Proto-Balto-Slavic *śweistei, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwéyt-ye-ti.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *ū́ˀdrāˀ; compare Latvian ûdrs, Old Prussian udro, Proto-Slavic *vỳdra (“otter”), from Proto-Indo-European *udreh₂, a substantivized feminine of *udrós (“aquatic, of water”). Compare Ancient Greek ὕδρα (húdra, “sea serpent”), Latin lutra (“otter”). The long vowel and acute ac
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *źámbas, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos. Cognate with Latvian zòbs (“tooth”) and Proto-Slavic *zǫbъ (“tooth”).

From Proto-Balto-Slavic [Term?], from Proto-Indo-European *ǵonh₂dʰos, *ǵn̥h₂dʰ-, cognate with Latvian zôds (“chin”) and Ancient Greek γνάθος (gnáthos, “jaw, point”); compare Proto-Indo-European *ǵénus (“jaw, chin, cheek”), whence Old Prussian żauna (“jaw”) and English chin.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *źémijāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰéǵʰōm. Compare Latvian zeme, Polish ziemia, Russian земля́ (zemljá), Persian زمین (zamin), Albanian dhe, Latin humus, Irish dú, Ancient Greek χθών (khthṓn). See also žmogus.

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *źibḗˀtei, cognate with Latvian zibēt (“to shine”), and further related to Latvian zibt (“to sparkle”), Latvian zibens (“lightning”). Further origin outside of Baltic unclear; the root hypothetically traces back to a Proto-Indo-European *ǵ⁽ʰ⁾e(y)b⁽ʰ⁾-, with no certain non-Bal
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *źeimā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰéyōm.

parole.significato: to know (be aware of; sure of)
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *źināˀtei, alternative form of *źnōˀtei; compare Latvian zinât (“know”), Old Prussian posinnat (“confess”), Proto-Slavic *znàti, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵn̥néh₃ti, from *ǵneh₃- (“to know”). The Baltic words are from the nasal-infixed present, *ǵn̥néh₃-, while the Slavic for

From Proto-Balto-Slavic *źū́ˀs; related to Latvian zivs, Old Prussian suckis (“fish”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰǵʰu-; cognate with Ancient Greek ἰχθῡ́ς (ikhthū́s), Old Armenian ձուկն (jukn, “fish”). Since *dK- regularly yielded *iKt- in Greek (compare ἰκτῖνος (iktînos), ἑκατόν (hekatón)), Proto-I
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *źwaisdā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰwoysdʰ-. Cognate to Samogitian žvaiždie, Latvian zvaigzne, Russian звезда (zvezda).
Inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *źwenˀgtei, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰweng-eti, from *ǵʰwen- “to sound, to make a sound”. Cognate include Latvian zviegt “to neigh, to whinny”.
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *źwēˀrís, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰwer-. Compare Russian зверь (zverʹ, “animal”), Latin ferus (“wild, savage”).
From Proto-Balto-Slavic *źansís, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰh₂éns.
